author: श्रीमदानन्दतीर्थभगवत्पादाचार्य
commentary:
कामात्मनां निन्दा कृता कथमेषाम् ? ‘स्वर्गकामो यजेत’ इत्यादौ कामस्यापि विहितत्वाद् इत्यत आह - कर्मण्येवेति ॥ 
 ‘ते’ इत्युपलक्षणार्थम् । तव ज्ञानिनोऽपि न फलकामकर्तव्यता; किम्वन्येषाम् ! न ‘त्वस्ति केषाञ्चिद्, न तेऽस्ति’ इति । स हि ज्ञानी नरांश इन्द्रश्च । मोहादिस्त्वभिभवादेः । यदि तेषां शुद्धसत्त्वानां न स्याज्ज्ञानम्, क्व अन्येषाम् ? उपदेशादेश्च सिद्धं ज्ञानं तेषाम् । ‘....पार्थार्ष्टिषेण....।’(भाग.२.७.४५) इत्यादिज्ञानिगणनाच्च । 

कामनिषेध एवात्र । फलानि ह्यस्वातन्त्र्येण भवन्ति । न हि कर्मफलानि कर्माभावे यत्नतोऽपि भवन्ति । भवन्ति च काम्यकर्मिणो विपर्ययप्रयत्नेऽपि अविरोधे । 

अतः कर्माकरणे एव प्रत्यवायः, न तु ज्ञानादिनाऽकामनया वा फलाप्राप्तौ । अतः कर्मण्येवाधिकारः । अतस्तदेव कार्यम्; न तु कामेन ज्ञानादिनिषेधेन वा फलप्राप्तिः । कामवचनानां तु तात्पर्यं भगवतैवोक्तम्- ‘रोचनार्थं फलश्रुतिः’(भाग.११.३.४७), ‘यथा भैषज्यरोचनम्’(भाग.११.२१.२३) इत्यादौ भागवते । 

अत एव ‘कामी यजेत’ इत्यर्थः; न तु ‘कामी भूत्वा’ इत्यर्थः । ‘निष्कामं ज्ञानपूर्वं च’(मनु.१२.८९) इति वचनात्, वक्ष्यमाणेभ्यश्च । ‘वसन्ते वसन्ते ज्योतिषा यजेत’ इत्यादिभ्यश्च । अतो मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूः । 
 कर्मफलं तत्कृतौ हेतुर्यस्य स कर्मफलहेतुः, स मा भूः । तर्हि न करोमि? इत्यत आह– मा त इति ॥ कर्माकरणे च स्नेहो माऽस्त्वित्यर्थः । अन्य(था)फलाभावेऽपि मत्प्रसादाख्यफलभावात् । इच्छा च तस्य युक्ता ‘वृणीमहे ते परितोषणाय’(भाग.४.३०.४०) इत्यादिमहदाचारात् । अनिन्दनात्, विशेषत इतरनिन्दनाच्च। सामान्यं विशेषो बाधत इति च प्रसिद्धम्– ‘सर्वान् आनय, नैकं मैत्रम्’ इत्यादौ । अतः - ‘नैकात्मतां मे स्पृहयन्ति केचिद्.....’(भाग.३.२६.३४), ‘भक्तिमन्विच्छन्तः’, ‘ब्रह्मजिज्ञासा’(ब्र,सू.१.१.१), 
 ‘विज्ञाय प्रज्ञां कुर्वीत.....’,(बृ.उ.६.४.२१)‘द्रष्टव्यः.....’ इत्यादिवचनेभ्यः, स्वार्थसेवकं प्रति न तथा स्नेहः, ‘किं ददामि’ इत्युक्ते सेवादियाचकं प्रति बहुतरः स्नेह इति लौकिकन्यायाच्च भक्तिज्ञानादिप्रार्थना कार्येति सिद्धम् ॥४७ ॥
translation:
Acharya Madhva addresses a brilliant logical contradiction here: If the Vedas explicitly tell us to perform certain rituals to reach heaven ('Svarga-kāmo yajeta'), why does Krishna heavily criticize desire-driven people (Kāmātmānaḥ) in the previous verses? Is Krishna contradicting the Vedas? - 

An objection is raised: 'Why has criticism been leveled against those whose nature is filled with material desires (Kāmātmānaḥ)?' For statements like 'He who desires heaven should perform sacrifices' are explicitly enjoined by Vedic law. To resolve this apparent contradiction, Krishna speaks the verse beginning with 'Karmaṇy-eva' (Your right is to action alone). The word Te (to you, Arjuna) is used as an illustrative indicator (Upalakṣaṇa). It means: 'If even for you, who are an enlightened soul (Jnani), it is an absolute non-duty to perform actions out of desire for fruits, what then to speak of ordinary, un-enlightened people! It is not that desire-driven action is acceptable for some and barred only for you. For Arjuna is a great Jnani, an amsha (partial manifestation) of Nara and Indra. His apparent delusion on the battlefield was merely a temporary eclipse caused by cosmic arrangement. If such pure, sattvic beings lacked true knowledge, where else could it possibly exist in ordinary men? Their perfect enlightenment is established by the fact that they receive instruction directly from the Lord and are explicitly counted among top-tier sages (Jnani-ganana) in texts like the Srimad Bhagavatam (2.7.45).

Therefore, the clear focus here is the absolute prohibition of selfish desires (Kāma-niṣedha). For the fruits of actions manifest entirely without your independent control (Asvātantryeṇa). Indeed, the fruits of an action can never come into existence if the action itself is missing, no matter how much external effort one applies. Conversely, if the cosmic laws are non-contradictory, the results still come to a person who acts selflessly, even if they explicitly try to avoid or reverse the material result. Therefore, the sin or spiritual downfall (Pratyavāya) lies strictly in the non-performance of duty (Karma-akaraṇa); it does not lie in the non-attainment of a material fruit due to acting with wisdom or selflessness. Hence, your authority and right reside exclusively in action. Therefore, duty alone must be executed. You should never seek the attainment of fruits through selfish desires or by rejecting spiritual wisdom. The true underlying purpose behind the desire-driven statements of the Vedas has been explicitly revealed by the Supreme Lord Himself in the Srimad Bhagavatam (11.3.47 and 11.21.23): 'The scriptural statements detailing material rewards are meant purely as a sweet inducement, exactly like sugar-coating a bitter medicine to make it appealing (Bhaiṣajya-rocanam).' Therefore, the phrase 'He who has desires should sacrifice' simply means: 'If you are currently trapped in material desires, channel them through a disciplined sacrifice to clear your mind'; it does not mean: 'You must actively cultivate desires and perform actions driven by them.' This is verified by the Manu Smriti (12.89): 'Actions should be executed selflessly and packed with spiritual knowledge,' as well as standard Vedic injunctions like 'Every spring season, one should perform the Jyotishtoma sacrifice [as an unalterable cycle of duty].' 

Therefore, 'Do not be the cause of the fruit of action.' A Karma-phala-hetu is a person whose sole driving motive to act is the material reward. Do not become such a calculator! An objection arises: 'If I cannot have the fruits, then I simply won't work!' To counter this, Krishna says: 'Mā te [saṅgo ’stv akarmaṇi]'—meaning: Let there be absolutely no affection or attachment toward lazy non-action. Because even when ordinary material rewards are completely absent, the grandest ultimate fruit—known as My Divine Grace (Mat-prasāda)—is explicitly present! And desiring this Divine Grace is perfectly justified and proper, as seen in the flawless behavior of great souls in the Srimad Bhagavatam (4.30.40): 'We only ask for that which brings complete satisfaction to You.' Desiring God's pleasure is never criticized; in fact, desiring anything other than His pleasure is heavily criticized. It is a well-known rule of logic that a specific rule (Vishesha) always overrides or refines a general rule (Samanya). For example, if one says: 'Bring everyone to the party (General), but do not bring Maitra (Specific).' 

Therefore, based on authoritative statements across the Brahma Sutras, Upanishads, and Bhagavatam such as: 'My pure devotees do not even desire oneness with Me,' 'Constantly seeking pure devotion,' 'Now, therefore, inquire into Brahman,' and 'The Supreme Lord must be seen and realized'. This is also proven by a simple worldly logic (Laukika-Nyaya): A master does not feel deep affection toward a selfish servant who only works to demand money. But a master feels immense, overwhelming affection toward a loving servant who steps forward and says, 'My dear master, what can I do to serve you today?' Therefore, it is definitively established (Siddham) that a soul must actively pray for nothing other than pure Devtion (Bhakti) and Spiritual Wisdom (Jnana)!
